title: US military ends long-running program to spot nuclear missile launches
gist: The US Space Force retired the Defense Support Program, the missile-warning satellite constellation flying since 1970, after its last two satellites moved to graveyard orbits in September 2026. Successor systems SBIRS and Next-Gen OPIR carry the early-warning mission.

themes.theme: End of the Defense Support Program

insights.claim: The US Space Force confirmed the retirement of the Defense Support Program in 2026 after its final two satellites (presumably DSP-20 and DSP-22) raised their orbits by a few hundred kilometers into graveyard orbits, ending more than 55 years of continuous space-based missile warning.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Marks a generational handover in US early-warning architecture, with fully commercial-era launch and bus approaches replacing bespoke Cold War satellites.
insights.quote: The DSP constellation was foundational to the defense of our nation,

insights.claim: DSP satellites evolved from about 1 metric ton with 2,000 infrared detectors in the initial 1970-73 block to about 2.5 tons with more than 6,000 detectors, flying to geosynchronous orbit and serving first against Soviet ICBMs and later against conventional threats like Iraqi Scud launches.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A benchmark for how infrared early-warning capability scaled and shifted from strategic to theater missions.

insights.claim: DSP satellites launched on a wide range of vehicles over decades, including Titan rockets, Delta IV Heavy and a space shuttle (DSP-16 on Atlantis in 1991), and the program's last launch was in 2007.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Illustrates how national-security launch demand has shifted across providers over time.

themes.theme: Successor systems: SBIRS and Next-Gen OPIR

insights.claim: The Space Based Infrared System, launched since 2011, has better sensors that generally detect dimmer events and give longer warning time than DSP, so the US is not flying blind after the retirement.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Warning capability does not drop with DSP's exit, so the retirement is not a near-term capability gap.
insights.locator: The United States is not flying blind

insights.claim: The first Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellite could launch within the next 12 months on a Vulcan rocket.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A near-term Vulcan national-security launch is a catalyst for ULA's manifest and for Next-Gen OPIR contractors.

insights.claim: The Air Force turned Space Launch Complex 40, used for Titan launches until 2005, over to then-small SpaceX in a competitive process hotly opposed by United Launch Alliance, illustrating how the military's launch supply base moved from incumbents to a startup.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Shows the structural share shift in national-security launch from incumbents to SpaceX.

insights.claim: The DSP program began when infrared observations were experimental and satellite manufacturing was bespoke, and the program's longevity was remarkable, with satellites flying operationally 55 years later.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Long-lived bespoke satellites contrast with today's shorter-cycle, proliferated approaches that drive replacement demand.
insights.quote: The program had a remarkable run in longevity.
